bill.title: To amend title XVIII of the Social Security Act to adjust payment for skin substitute products under the Medicare program.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

classification.plainSummary: This bill would change how Medicare pays for skin substitute products, which are medical materials used to treat wounds and burns. The bill amends the Social Security Act to adjust the payment structure for these products under the Medicare program. The source material does not provide detail on the specific nature of the payment adjustment or whether it increases or decreases reimbursement rates.

industries.rationale: Manufacturers of skin substitute products would see their Medicare reimbursement rates adjusted by this bill.
Hospitals and physician groups that apply skin substitutes would be affected by changes to Medicare payment rates for these products.

plain.whatItDoes: No one has written a summary of this bill yet. All we have is its title, and a title is not a description of a law. To find out what it does, you have to open the bill itself.
plain.everydayEffect: Nothing has changed yet. The title alone does not say what would change for you, and this tool will not guess. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: From the bill title, and from the subject labels that library staff put on it. There is no official summary of this bill yet.
plain.titleInPlainWords: Would change Medicare rules so that they adjust payment for skin substitute products under the Medicare program.

method.formula: score = Σ_industries ( donorShare(industry) × billWeight(industry) ), where billWeight = classifierConfidence / Σ classifierConfidence. Range 0–1, read as a weighted share of disclosed itemized money.

ordinary.text: They wrote this bill. Sponsoring a bill about your own district's industry is the ordinary case, not the odd one.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
